title: Measuring How Cells Stick, Pull, and Travel
endLine: Measure grip, pull, or travel directly; no assay proves every step.

scenes.tts: How do you measure how hard a cell sticks, pulls, or travels? A still picture only shows where cells sit. Living cell assays turn invisible grip, force, and travel into direct measurements.
scenes.caption: How do you measure how hard a cell sticks, pulls, or travels? A still picture only shows where cells sit. Living cell assays turn invisible grip, force, and travel into direct measurements.
scenes.visual: A dark, high-contrast tissue chamber fills 70% of the frame height, holding glowing cells on a pale gridded substrate (schematic). The frame starts frozen, then unlocks as the opening question begins: cells on the left clump together, a central cell tugs the substrate grid beneath it, and a cell on the right crawls toward the far edge. Three high-contrast labels appear one by one beside each motion: 'Stick', 'Pull', 'Travel'.
scenes.narration: How do you measure how hard a cell sticks, pulls, or travels? A still picture only shows where cells sit. Living cell assays turn invisible grip, force, and travel into direct measurements.

scenes.visual: The same living chamber continues with gentle ambient motion—cells softly pulsing and drifting—while the title 'Measuring How Cells Stick, Pull, and Travel' fades in near the top and fades out.

scenes.tts: Start with sticking. Separate cells and watch if they clump back together: a reaggregation assay. Every anchoring grip uses four links: outer partner, receptor, internal adaptors, and inner cable. To test a link, remove or block it, watch clumping change, then restore it.
scenes.caption: Start with sticking. Separate cells and watch if they clump back together: a reaggregation assay. Every anchoring grip uses four links: outer partner, receptor, internal adaptors, and inner cable. To test a link, remove or block it, watch clumping change, then restore it.
scenes.visual: In the same chamber, a cell cluster separates into single glowing spheres that drift and snap back into a compact clump ('Reaggregation', schematic). A zoom ring magnifies one cell-to-cell contact into a four-link geometric chain—no molecular structures—labelled 'Partner', 'Receptor', 'Adaptor', and 'Cable' (schematic). The adaptor block fades out and the cells drift apart; dropping the adaptor block back in reconnects the chain and snaps the cells tightly together.
scenes.narration: Start with sticking. Separate cells and watch if they clump back together: a reaggregation assay. Every anchoring grip uses four links: outer partner, receptor, internal adaptors, and inner cable. To test a link, remove or block it, watch clumping change, then restore it.

scenes.tts: Sticking also powers crawling: protrusion, grip, contraction, and release. Integrin receptors and linker proteins form focal adhesions, anchoring cells to their substrate. Filament growth is the engine, and adhesion is the clutch. Mechanics assays measure traction stress, force per area on the substrate, alongside local actin speed.
scenes.caption: Sticking also powers crawling: protrusion, grip, contraction, and release. Integrin receptors and linker proteins form focal adhesions, anchoring cells to their substrate. Filament growth is the engine, and adhesion is the clutch. Mechanics assays measure traction stress, force per area on the substrate, alongside local actin speed.
scenes.visual: The zoom ring closes onto one cell flattened on the chamber's gridded substrate (schematic). As each step is spoken, the cell pushes its leading edge right ('Protrusion'), bright anchor pads lock onto the grid ('Focal adhesion'), internal actin lines flow rearward while the cell pulls the grid inward ('Contraction'), and rear pads detach ('Release'). Force arrows appear under the anchor pads ('Traction stress', schematic) beside a speed gauge on the flowing actin cables (schematic).
scenes.narration: Sticking also powers crawling: protrusion, grip, contraction, and release. Integrin receptors and linker proteins form focal adhesions, anchoring cells to their substrate. Filament growth is the engine, and adhesion is the clutch. Mechanics assays measure traction stress, force per area on the substrate, alongside local actin speed.

scenes.tts: Inside developing tissue, biologists track where living cells travel. A dye like D i I or D i A dissolves into cell membranes. Cells leaving that spot carry it along. Slices let you watch cells move; grafts show what they become. Each assay measures one thing directly: grip, pull, or travel.
scenes.caption: Inside developing tissue, biologists track where living cells travel. A dye like DiI or DiA dissolves into cell membranes. Cells leaving that spot carry it along. Slices let you watch cells move; grafts show what they become. Each assay measures one thing directly: grip, pull, or travel.
scenes.visual: The chamber's substrate floor stretches smoothly into a schematic cross-section of developing forebrain tissue: ventral eminences on the left, cortex curving across the upper right. A glowing drop of dye ('DiI / DiA') touches one spot on the left; individual coloured cells detach and stream sideways toward the cortex (schematic). Two small corner icons follow: a thin 'slice' with moving cells, and a 'graft' whose cells take on neuron shapes (schematic). Along the bottom edge, three simple icons—grip, pull, travel—highlight one at a time while the other two remain dim.

scenes.tts: Back to the crawling cell. Focal adhesions anchor its forward pull. Suppose you make those adhesions much stronger. Will the cell always crawl faster, or can stronger adhesion slow migration down?
scenes.caption: Back to the crawling cell. Focal adhesions anchor its forward pull. Suppose you make those adhesions much stronger. Will the cell always crawl faster, or can stronger adhesion slow migration down?
scenes.visual: The tissue cross-section transforms smoothly back to the crawling cell on the gridded substrate (schematic). Its focal adhesion pads brighten and widen, gripping the grid tightly as the front pushes forward. A high-contrast question appears above the cell: 'Stronger adhesion: faster crawling, or slower?'
scenes.narration: Back to the crawling cell. Focal adhesions anchor its forward pull. Suppose you make those adhesions much stronger. Will the cell always crawl faster, or can stronger adhesion slow migration down?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen for 4.5 seconds of silence. Ambient motion continues: the cell's front edge stretches right while bright rear adhesion pads tug hard against the substrate grid without letting go (schematic).

scenes.tts: Stronger adhesion can slow migration, because the rear must let go, and stronger grip resists that release. In P t K 1 cells, traction stress and local actin speed had a two-part relationship. It changed near eight to ten nanometres per second. So faster flow does not always mean more traction; the clutch is only a starting model.
scenes.caption: Stronger adhesion can slow migration, because the rear must let go, and stronger grip resists that release. In PtK1 cells, traction stress and local actin speed had a two-part relationship. It changed near 8 to 10 nm/s. So faster flow does not always mean more traction; the clutch is only a starting model.
scenes.visual: The question fades out. On the crawling cell, bright rear pads stay pinned to the grid so the tail stalls ('Rear must release', schematic). Beside the cell, a schematic graph plots local actin speed horizontally against traction stress vertically, showing a two-part curve that bends at a marker labelled '8–10 nm/s' ('Schematic') where faster flow no longer increases traction.
scenes.narration: Stronger adhesion can slow migration, because the rear must let go, and stronger grip resists that release. In PtK1 cells, traction stress and local actin speed had a two-part relationship. It changed near 8 to 10 nm/s. So faster flow does not always mean more traction; the clutch is only a starting model.

scenes.tts: Every assay has limits. Reaggregation tests clumping, not force on one contact. Dye tracking follows moving cells, but does not show what they become. When losing a gene halts migration, two ideas compete. It may be needed in migrating cells, or in the tissue they cross.
scenes.caption: Every assay has limits. Reaggregation tests clumping, not force on one contact. Dye tracking follows moving cells, but does not show what they become. When losing a gene halts migration, two ideas compete. It may be needed in migrating cells, or in the tissue they cross.
scenes.visual: In the same carried chamber, three brief limit checks animate in sequence (schematic): first, a clumped cell ball gets a question mark over one contact ('No single-contact force'); next, dyed cells crossing the tissue get a question mark over their fate ('Identity unproven'); finally, a stalled migrating cell blinks alternately with the tissue beneath it ('In traveller?' vs 'In tissue?').
scenes.narration: Every assay has limits. Reaggregation tests clumping, not force on one contact. Dye tracking follows moving cells, but does not show what they become. When losing a gene halts migration, two ideas compete. It may be needed in migrating cells, or in the tissue they cross.

scenes.tts: These assays unlocked discoveries. In 1992, Hirano and colleagues studied P C 9 cells carrying the receptor E-cadherin. Calcium-dependent aggregation was greatly reduced, and cells grew mostly singly. Putting the adaptor alpha-catenin back restored firm, compact aggregates. Binding outside is not enough for strong adhesion.
scenes.caption: These assays unlocked discoveries. In 1992, Hirano and colleagues studied PC9 cells carrying the receptor E-cadherin. Calcium-dependent aggregation was greatly reduced, and cells grew mostly singly. Putting the adaptor α-catenin back restored firm, compact aggregates. Binding outside is not enough for strong adhesion.
scenes.visual: The chamber returns to scattered PC9 cells whose outer E-cadherin blocks touch yet fail to hold ('Hirano et al., 1992', schematic). Dropping the inner adaptor block ('α-catenin') into each cell's four-link chain snaps the single cells together into firm, compact aggregates.
scenes.narration: These assays unlocked discoveries. In 1992, Hirano and colleagues studied PC9 cells carrying the receptor E-cadherin. Calcium-dependent aggregation was greatly reduced, and cells grew mostly singly. Putting the adaptor α-catenin back restored firm, compact aggregates. scenes.tts: In 1996, de Carlos, López-Mascaraque and Valverde dyed the lateral ganglionic eminence, a ventral forebrain region, in cultured rat embryos. Most labelled cells settled nearby in ventrolateral cortex. Others ran sideways, tangentially, into the preplate, the first layer of young cortical neurons.

scenes.visual: The chamber stretches back into the schematic developing-forebrain cross-section ('de Carlos et al., 1996'). Dye appears in the lateral ganglionic eminence on the left: most glowing cells travel short radial paths into the nearby ventrolateral cortex, while a distinct group streams tangentially into the thin upper cortical preplate (schematic).
scenes.narration: In 1996, de Carlos, López-Mascaraque and Valverde dyed the lateral ganglionic eminence, a ventral forebrain region, in cultured rat embryos. scenes.tts: In 1999, Wichterle, Alvarez-Buylla and colleagues tracked cells from another eminence, the M G E. In embryonic slices, those cells migrated extensively toward the cortex, and grafted cells became neurons. Each assay captures one living step, and shows what still needs another test.

scenes.visual: In the same schematic brain slice ('Wichterle et al., 1999'), glowing cells leave a second ventral eminence labelled 'MGE' and stream extensively across into the cortex; an inset ring shows grafted MGE cells sprouting branched neuron shapes (schematic). The slice gently dims into the live chamber background.

scenes.visual: Clean silent end card over the dark chamber background displaying the core rule in large high-contrast type: 'Measure grip, pull, or travel directly; no assay proves every step.'
